findings.title: The sudoers rule does not authorize the repair/verify command the cutover runs
findings.description:
The file's own header claims it contains "Exactly the commands those scripts issue, nothing wider". `_repair()` (`scripts/cutover_921_minute_sessions.py:93-100`) runs `sudo /opt/manta-trading/.venv/bin/python scripts/repair_921_minute_sessions.py <mode>` — with `sudo=True` — and that command appears in none of `MT_UNITS`, `MT_RUN`, `MT_INSTALL`, `MT_READ`, or `MT_GIT`. On a host where this file is the operator account's only grant, the cutover's very first repair step (`_repair("--check")`) is refused, because sudoers is allow-list: an unlisted command is denied rather than password-prompted. `sudo -v`, `sudo -u manta-trading git -C /opt/manta-trading rev-parse HEAD` (line 14, matching `cutover_common.install`), `sudo cat /etc/manta-trading.env` (`cutover_common.migrate`), and `sudo systemctl stop/start mt-*` are all covered, so the omission of the repair invocation looks unintentional rather than a deliberate narrowing.

Two related couplings worth pinning while you are here: `MT_INSTALL` hard-codes `/home/manta/source/repos/manta/trading-data/deploy/install-production.sh`, and `cutover_common.install()` now resolves that path as `Path(__file__).resolve().parents[1] / "deploy/install-production.sh"` (`scripts/cutover_common.py:132-135`) — nothing checks that the two agree, so a checkout at any other path breaks the install step silently; and this artifact has no drift guard, although the repo already guards its sibling deploy artifacts (`test/unit/deploy/test_units.py` parses the units, the installer's `UNITS` array and `mt-run`). A guard in that module asserting every `sudo`-prefixed command the cutover scripts issue is named by a `Cmnd_Alias` in this file would have caught this omission mechanically.

findings.title: The new cagg-freshness probe drops the `-infinity` normalization slice 168 documents as required
findings.description:
`cagg_freshness_for_session` selects `stats.last_successful_finish` raw. `src/manta_trading/market/maintenance/cagg_freshness.py:68-79` states in the same repository: "`last_successful_finish` is `-infinity` for a policy that has been created but has never completed a run. psycopg cannot load that into a datetime — it raises `DataError` mid-fetch", and normalizes it with `nullif(s.last_successful_finish, '-infinity'::timestamptz)`. The new query has no such guard, so for any cagg whose refresh policy has not yet completed a run (a fresh or rebuilt database — 051 recreates both coverage caggs' policies, and the test tier runs against freshly migrated databases) the fetch raises. `run_verify` (`scripts/repair_921_minute_sessions.py:255-295`) and `main` catch only `RepairScanTimeout`, so the operator gets a psycopg traceback instead of the `[WAIT]`/`[FAIL]` verdict, and `cutover_921`'s `_verify_when_fresh` never sees the text it branches on.

The same probe also re-spells `'policy_refresh_continuous_aggregate'` as a bare literal in the SQL, while `cagg_freshness.py:58` defines that value as a named constant precisely because it is "the same value `cagg_repair.py` filters on" — the project rule is one definition per value.

findings.title: A chunk with bars but no judgeable session keeps `PARTIAL`, contradicting the stated removal of the weekend tolerance
findings.description:
`judge_chunk_by_sessions` returns the classifier's verdict unchanged when `judged` is empty. `src/manta_trading/data/acquisition/daemon/minute.py:889-901` justifies deleting the old four-day tolerance with "a weekend or holiday tail has no session to be missing, so a chunk whose sessions are all covered is SUCCESS however far its last bar sits before chunk_end" — but a chunk containing *no* session at all is the case where "all its sessions are covered" is vacuously true, and there the code does not return `SUCCESS`.

Concretely: for a range lying wholly between two sessions (the shape a legacy midnight-anchored row takes, e.g. `[Sat 00:00, Sun 00:00]`), `fetch_session_bounds` returns `{}`, so `judged` is empty and a response carrying only the spillover bar keeps the classifier's `PARTIAL`. The removed tolerance (`(chunk_end.date() - latest.date()).days <= 4`) turned exactly that response into `SUCCESS`, which deleted the row. Now the row survives, is re-picked each cycle (it is the most recent actionable gap), and `_advance_minute_gap` increments `attempt_count` each time until it promotes to `RETRY_EXHAUSTED` at `MAX_RETRY_COUNT` — a terminal row that makes `data_status.health` read `FAILED` for that symbol forever, which is the "a unit that is always failed is not an alarm" pathology slice 921 exists to remove.

The behaviour is deliberate and pinned by `test_no_judgeable_session_keeps_the_classifier_verdict` and `test_empty_bounds_judge_nothing`, and the reachable population may now be small because the repair resets in-window rows to session-close ends. I could not verify how many legacy midnight-anchored actionable rows remain in production (`find_truncated_days` and `build_truncated_day_index` ignore them; `count_row_shapes`' `midnight_ended_rows` counter is the only measurement, and terminal legacy rows are excluded from `pick_most_recent_actionable_gap`). Please either confirm the class is empty in production, or state the residual — currently the code comment asserts a property the code does not have for this input.

findings.title: The narration log does not contain the acceptance output it exists to preserve
findings.description: `start_log`/`say` (`scripts/cutover_common.py:41-62`) tee only `say()` lines. The cutover's `_repair()` prints the `--check`/`--apply`/`--verify` bodies with a plain `print(output)`, never `say`, so the numbers the whole slice is judged on are absent from `project-documents/user/notes/921-cutover-<ts>.log`. The same is true of `install()`, `hold_timer()`, `release_timer()` and the "`unit` is running — waiting" polls in `cutover_common`, which all use `print`. The script's closing line tells the operator `full narration: {log_path}`, and the incomplete-run line tells them to "read the FAIL lines" — those FAIL lines are in the terminal and not in the file. The added test (`test_say_tees_to_the_log_file`) asserts only the `say` path, so this gap is invisible to the suite. Given the docstring's premise ("The first 921 cutover's only record was terminal scrollback across two ten-hour firings"), routing the repair/verify output through the log is the point.

findings.title: The minute-pass timer still describes a 30-minute stagger that no longer exists
findings.description: The `Description` (line 2) and the `[Timer]` comment (lines 6-7) say the pass is "staggered 30 minutes behind the daily pass" so the two "never start simultaneously". With the first firing moved to `04:05` and `mt-daily-pass.timer` at `00:35/12:35`, the first firing is 3 h 30 min behind, not 30 minutes; only the `13:05` firing is 30 minutes behind `12:35`. The diff updated the equivalent comment in `deploy/systemd/mt-kalshi-pass.timer` ("00:35/12:35, 04:05/13:05") but left this one stating a schedule the file no longer has — in the file whose firing time the health check's judged-session boundary is derived from.

findings.title: `bar_timestamp` misses `OSError`, which `datetime.fromtimestamp` is documented to raise
findings.description: The docstring promises "A bar without a readable timestamp cannot satisfy any session", and the `except` tuple is `(ValueError, TypeError, OverflowError)`. `datetime.fromtimestamp` also raises `OSError` when the C `gmtime`/`localtime` call fails for an out-of-range value, so an absurd epoch from the provider escapes as an exception from `judge_chunk_by_sessions`, is caught by `_process_minute_symbol`'s last-resort handler and mis-tagged `MinuteFailureKind.DATABASE` — the same misattribution the class docstring says must not happen. The pre-existing `_bar_to_row` (`minute.py`) has the same exposure, so this mirrors an existing pattern rather than introducing a new one; adding `OSError` (or a range bound) closes it in both places.

findings.title: `MT_READ` grants the operator account root-level read of the production credentials
findings.description: `Cmnd_Alias MT_READ = /usr/bin/cat /etc/manta-trading.env` exists so `cutover_common.migrate()` can compare the checkout's maintenance URL with the production one (`verify_migrate_target`). The rule is correctly scoped to a single file, but the file it exposes is the whole credential set — DB URL, API keys — to an unprivileged account, passwordlessly. A helper that prints only `(host, port, dbname)` would satisfy the same guard with a fraction of the blast radius. Flagging for visibility, not as a blocker.

findings.title: Import ordering in the new `minute.py` block is not isort-conformant
findings.description: `ruff` is configured with the `I` rule set (`pyproject.toml`), and the new imports introduce a fresh inversion inside one contiguous block: `...gaps.repair_921` (line 60) precedes `...gaps.minute_coverage` (line 64), and `...daemon.minute_sessions` (line 56) sits between `manta_trading.data.gaps` and `manta_trading.data.gaps.compute_missing_ranges`. Sorted order would be `gaps` → `gaps.compute_missing_ranges` → `gaps.minute_coverage` → `gaps.repair_921`, with the `acquisition.*` imports ahead of all of them. The file was already out of order around this block before the change, so this is not making a green tree red — but since the new lines are contiguous and mechanical to fix, `ruff check --select I --fix` on this file is worth a follow-up.
